tagline.text: Bamboo rafts on an emerald river between white limestone cliffs

children.text: A national park at the foot of the Sierra Madre in General Tinio, Nueva Ecija, where the Peñaranda River flows between white limestone cliffs a dozen-odd meters high. A day trip near Manila for riding bamboo rafts up and down the emerald river and exploring a suspension bridge and viewpoint.
Minalungao National Park is in Pias village, General Tinio, Nueva Ecija, about

north of Manila. Set at the foot of the Sierra Madre range bordering Doña Remedios Trinidad in Bulacan province, the roughly 2,018-hectare protected area stretches along the Peñaranda River. It became a national park under Republic Act No. 5100 in

The star here is the screen of limestone cliffs standing on both sides of the river. Smoothed by the water, the white rock rises to around 16 meters, forming a narrow gorge, through which the river flows slowly, glowing green and turquoise in the sunlight. Bamboo rafts called "balsa" travel up and down this gorge, and a long suspension bridge spans the river, offering a fine view looking down from above.

The name "Minalungao" is said to mean "gold mine in a cave," and indeed small caves riddle the cliffs here and there. General Tinio was a farming town called "Papaya" until 1957, and it's also known as the Philippine town with the most brass bands. The park is developed as an eco-tourism site by the local government, and the riverbank has a cluster of bamboo huts, small shops, and a raft landing.

With cheap admission and raft fees and just over three hours' drive from Manila, it suits families and groups of friends who want to enjoy the water in nature without elaborate preparation. That said, the river fills with crowds on summer peak-season weekends and Black Saturday during Holy Week, so if you want the cliffs and river at their quietest, a weekday morning is best.

Riding a bamboo raft, poled along by a boatman, up and down the gorge between the cliffs is Minalungao's signature experience. Rent a roofed raft and you can even eat a packed lunch on the water while staying out of the sun.

In the dry season, the Peñaranda River is clear enough to see the bottom, with a vivid green color. Swim in the shallow edges, but be sure to wear a life vest, since there are plenty of deep spots. Life vests can be rented on-site.

blocks.title: Looking down on the gorge from the suspension bridge

children.text: Standing on the long suspension bridge across the river, you get the whole scene at once — the white cliffs, the green river, and the rafts drifting below. It sways a little, so cross slowly.

blocks.title: The cross viewpoint at the top of the stairs

children.text: A long, steep staircase from the riverbank leads up to a hilltop viewpoint marked by a cross. It looks out over the gorge and the foothills of the Sierra Madre, and climbing at sunrise or late afternoon means less heat.
Take a raft upstream and you'll see rock arches carved by the water and small caves cut into the cliffs. The caves are dark and slippery inside, so follow your boatman's guidance.
The river has a rock ledge about
high where you can watch local young men jump in. It's dangerous for visitors to try, so it's best to simply watch.
Renting a bamboo hut on the riverbank and spending half a day eating food you brought is the local way to enjoy the park. Some spots let you use a grill.

In the wet season,
June–October

, rain in the upstream mountains often raises the river and turns it muddy. When the current gets strong, rafting and swimming are suspended, and the water stays cloudy for days after a typhoon passes. During this period, check notices from the park or General Tinio's tourism office before you go, and finish swimming in the morning before afternoon thunderstorms arrive.

Minalungao is a day-trip spot, so there's no proper lodging inside the park. If you want to stay overnight and see more of the area, use a hotel or resort in downtown Gapan or Cabanatuan (about
per night). Gapan has Nueva Ecija's oldest church, built in the 19th century, and an old mansion street, good for an evening walk.

Shops at the park entrance and riverbank mostly sell drinks, instant noodles, and simple snacks and fried food. Locals often buy grilled chicken, pork, rice, and fruit from the Gapan or General Tinio market and share it at a hut, and it's easiest to do the same. Nueva Ecija is the Philippines' largest rice-producing province and also known for processing carabao milk, so it's worth picking up pastillas and cheese made from carabao milk on your way back. Gapan and downtown Cabanatuan have malls and chain restaurants, convenient for a late lunch or dinner somewhere air-conditioned after swimming.
Settle the time and route for your raft first, then negotiate the fare. The more people share a raft, the lower the cost per person.
It's best to arrive around
, when there are fewer people and the water color is at its finest. Group visitors increase after lunch.
Bring clothes you don't mind getting wet, a change of clothes, aqua shoes, a dry bag, and a towel. Changing rooms and showers are basic.
There's no ATM around the park, and only cash is accepted. Bring plenty of small bills from Gapan.
Midday sun reflecting off the cliffs gets very hot. You'll need a hat, sunscreen, and plenty of water.
The water color photographs best from late morning into midday, when the sun reaches down into the gorge.
Phone signal weakens inside the gorge. Set a pickup time with your tricycle driver, and agree on a meeting spot with your group in advance.
Carry all your trash back out. It's also best to avoid using shampoo or soap in the river, to help keep the water clear.
The river suddenly deepens toward the base of the cliffs, and in some spots the current runs invisibly strong. Wear a life vest regardless of your swimming ability, and avoid diving off high rocks.
If it rains or the water turns muddy during the wet season, get out of the water immediately. Rain upstream can raise the water level quickly.
Limestone rocks and the stairs get very slippery when wet. Shoes with firm soles are safer than sandals.
The suspension bridge and rafts have posted capacity limits — follow them, and don't horse around or bunch up on one side of a raft.
Entrance fees and operating rules can change under local government policy, so check the latest notices.
On crowded days, keep a close eye on belongings left at your hut, and it's best not to bring valuables at all.
